verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} new{H2319} heavens{H8064} and a new{H2319} ground{H127}, for the first{H7223} heavens{H8064} and the earth{H776} had expired{H1478}, and the sea{H3220} was no{H3808} more{H5750}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֲדָמָה (adamah, H127 — 'ground/soil') for the NEW earth but אֶרֶץ (erets, H776) for the OLD earth. Greek uses γῆ (ge) for both. No translator going Greek→Hebrew would use two different words where Greek has one. The adamah echoes Genesis 2:7 — man formed from adamah returns to renewed adamah.

Uses יִגְוַע (yigva, H1478 — 'expired/died') — the verb used when patriarchs die (Gen 25:8, 25:17, 35:29, 49:33). The earth 'dies' like a person. Greek παρῆλθεν means merely 'passed away.' A back-translator would use עָבַר (avar — 'passed'), not the biological death verb גוע.
greek_deviations: Greek παρῆλθεν ('passed away') is far weaker than Hebrew יגוע ('expired/died'). The Hebrew verb implies biological death of the old creation.
translation_notes: 'Ground' for adamah (not 'earth') to preserve the distinction from erets. The adamah/erets contrast is theologically loaded: adamah is the soil from which Adam was formed (Gen 2:7), the soil cursed for Adam's sake (Gen 3:17), now renewed.
'Expired' for yigva to capture the Hebrew verb's specific meaning of biological death, distinguishing it from merely 'passing away.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 65:17 prophesies 'new heavens and a new earth' using שָׁמַיִם חֲדָשִׁים וָאָרֶץ חֲדָשָׁה — with erets for both old and new. This Hebrew text's switch to adamah is a deliberate theological choice.

verses.translation: And I, Yochanan{H3110}, saw{H7200} the holy{H6918} city{H5892}, the new{H2319} Yerushalayim{H3389}, descending{H3381} from the heavens{H8064} to the earth{H776}; and it was adorned like a woman{H802} adorned before{H6440} her lord{H1167}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אִשָּׁה (ishah — 'woman/wife', H802) not כַּלָּה (kalah — 'bride'). Greek has νύμφην (bride). A back-translator from Greek would use kalah. The Hebrew author uses the more general 'woman' for the simile.

'From the heavens to the earth' (מִשָּׁמַיִם לָאָרֶץ) — Greek has 'from God out of heaven' (ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). The Hebrew gives the trajectory (heaven→earth); the Greek gives the source (from God). These are different perspectives a translator would not interchange.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἡτοιμασμένην ('prepared') before 'adorned' — absent in Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'adorned,' not 'prepared and adorned.'
Greek says 'from God' (ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ) which the Hebrew omits entirely.
translation_notes: 'Lord' for ba'al (H1167) captures the ownership/authority nuance. Ba'al means 'master/owner/lord' and is the standard Hebrew word for 'husband' that emphasizes his headship role.
מְקֻשָּׁט (mequshat) is from a root meaning 'adorn/decorate,' common in later Hebrew and Aramaic but not in the standard OT lexicon. No Strong's number assigned.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} a great{H1419} voice{H6963} from the throne{H3678} which said{H559}: See{H7200}! The dwelling-place{H4908} of YHWH{H3068} is beside{H681} the man{H120}, and he shall be Elohim{H430} to them, and they shall be a people{H5971} to him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִשְׁכַּן (mishkan, H4908) — the specific word for the Tabernacle of Moses (Ex 25:9, 26:1ff). Greek σκηνή is generic 'tent.' A Hebrew author naturally reaches for the Torah's technical term; a back-translator might use אֹהֶל (ohel — tent) or just transliterate.

Uses singular הָאָדָם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120) with the definite article, echoing Genesis where God walked with 'the adam.' Greek has plural τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('men'). A back-translator from Greek would write אנשים (anashim — 'men'), not the Genesis-laden ha-adam.
Uses אֵצֶל (etsel, H681 — 'beside/next to') — a word expressing physical proximity. Greek μετά ('with') is far more generic. No back-translator would choose etsel from meta.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: voice 'from the throne' (מהכסא). Greek: voice 'from heaven' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ). Major difference in the source of the voice.

Greek adds σκηνώσει μετ' αὐτῶν ('he will dwell/tabernacle with them') and καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ θεὸς ἔσται μετ' αὐτῶν θεὸς αὐτῶν ('and God himself will be with them, their God') — expanded clauses absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Dwelling-place' for mishkan preserves the Tabernacle connection without anachronistically saying 'tabernacle.'
'Beside' for etsel captures the spatial intimacy — not merely 'with' but positioned right next to.
textual_notes: The covenant formula 'I will be their Elohim and they shall be my people' appears in Jer 31:33, Ezek 37:27, Zech 8:8. The Hebrew naturally uses the OT covenant language.

verses.translation: And YHWH{H3068} Elohim{H430} shall wipe{H4229} a tear{H1832} from upon all{H3605} faces{H6440}, and the death{H4194} shall not rule{H4910} anymore{H5750}; nor any distress or outcries{H6818} or afflictions, for the former{H7223} has passed{H5674}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 25:8: וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים — 'And the Lord YHWH will wipe a tear from upon all faces.' The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact phrasing 'from upon all faces' (מעל כל פנים). Greek changes this to 'every tear from their eyes' (πᾶν δάκρυον ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). A back-translator from Greek would write כל דמעה מעיניהם, not the Isaiah quote.

Uses יִמְשֹׁל (yimshol — 'shall rule/reign', H4910) for death. Greek has οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι ('shall be no more'). A back-translator from Greek would write לא יהיה עוד ('shall be no more'), using היה (to be), not משל (to rule). The Hebrew says death's REIGN ends — not that death ceases to exist.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a tear from upon all faces' (Isaiah 25:8 verbatim). Greek: 'every tear from their eyes' — a loose paraphrase that loses the Isaiah source.
Hebrew: 'death shall not rule anymore.' Greek: 'death shall be no more.' Fundamentally different claims — the end of death's dominion vs. the end of death's existence.
translation_notes: 'Rule' for yimshol is critical — this aligns with Romans 5:14,17 where death 'reigned' (ἐβασίλευσεν) and 1 Cor 15:26 where death is 'destroyed' (defeated) not annihilated.
צַעַר (tsa'ar — distress) and עִנּוּיִם (innuyim — afflictions) lack standard Strong's numbers; they are post-biblical Hebrew forms.
textual_notes: The Isaiah 25:8 parallel is the strongest OT connection in this verse. The Hebrew author quotes it verbatim; the Greek translator paraphrased it.

verses.translation: And the one sitting{H3427} upon the throne{H3678} said{H559}: See{H7200}! I have made{H6213} all{H3605} things new{H2319}. And he said{H559} to me: Write{H3789}, for these words{H1697} are truth{H571}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses past tense עָשִׂיתִי (asiti — 'I have made', perfect tense). Greek has present tense ποιῶ ('I make/am making'). Hebrew perfect tense presents the renewal as already accomplished from God's perspective — a completed act. The Greek present tense suggests an ongoing process. These are fundamentally different theological perspectives that cannot be reconciled as translation variants.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truth' (אֱמֶת, singular). Greek: 'true and faithful' (ἀληθινοὶ καὶ πιστοί). Greek adds 'faithful' (πιστοί) which is absent from the Hebrew.

Hebrew: אֱמֶת הִיא — 'truth she is' (feminine singular, referring to the collected words as a unit). Greek: ἀληθινοὶ καὶ πιστοί εἰσιν — 'true and faithful they are' (masculine plural). Different gender and number.
translation_notes: 'Have made' (past tense) for asiti — this is the Hebrew perfect, indicating completed action. The divine perspective sees the renewal as already done.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: All{H3605} has passed{H5674}. I am the first{H7223} and the last{H314}, the beginning and the end{H5490}. And I will give{H5414} to the thirsty{H6771} living{H2416} waters{H4325}, freely{H2600}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew has הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') — a direct quote from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 where YHWH declares 'I am the first, and I am the last.' Greek has τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω ('the Alpha and the Omega') — Greek letters. If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write האלף והתו ('the Aleph and the Tav'). Instead, the Hebrew preserves the Isaiah quotation. The Greek translator converted the Hebrew concept to Greek letters. This is among the strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation.

Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') — a specific Hebrew idiom for flowing spring water (Jer 2:13, 17:13; Zech 14:8; Gen 26:19). Greek has τῆς πηγῆς τοῦ ὕδατος τῆς ζωῆς ('the fountain of the water of life'). A back-translator from Greek would write מעין מים החיים ('fountain of the waters of life'), not the idiomatic mayim chayyim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the first and the last' (Isaiah quote). Greek: 'the Alpha and the Omega' (Greek letter metaphor). Entirely different expressions.
Hebrew: 'living waters' (two words). Greek: 'the fountain of the water of life' (expanded phrase).
translation_notes: תְּחִילַּת (techilat — 'beginning') lacks a standard Strong's number; it's a later Hebrew form from the root חלל.

'Living waters' is the idiomatic English rendering of mayim chayyim — water that flows (as opposed to stagnant cistern water). See Jeremiah 2:13 where YHWH calls himself 'the fountain of living waters.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — 'Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, YHWH of hosts: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.' The speaker on the throne uses YHWH's own self-declaration from Isaiah.

verses.translation: Whoever overcomes{H5329} shall be an heir{H3423} of all{H3605}, and I shall be Elohim{H430} to him, and he shall be a son{H1121} to me.

translation_notes: אֶהְיֶה (ehyeh — 'I shall be') appears in brackets [אֶהְיֶה] in the source text, suggesting editorial restoration. This is the same form God uses in Exodus 3:14 (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — 'I will be what I will be').
'Heir' for yoresh (H3423) — the root ירש means to possess/inherit, used of Israel inheriting the Promised Land.
textual_notes: Echoes 2 Samuel 7:14 — 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son.' The Davidic covenant promise extended to all overcomers.

verses.translation: But to those who do not believe{H539}, and to murderers{H7523}, and to fornicators{H2181}, and to sorcerers{H3784}, and to liars, I will give{H5414} their wages{H7939} from the fire{H784} of Sheol{H7585} which burns{H8313} with fire{H784} and sulfur{H1614}; and this is the second{H8145} death{H4194}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׂכָרָם (secharam — 'their wages', H7939). Greek has τὸ μέρος αὐτῶν ('their portion/part'). A back-translator from Greek would use חֵלֶק (cheleq — 'portion'), not שָׂכָר (sachar — 'wage'). The Hebrew implies payment earned by deeds; the Greek implies an allotted share.

CRITICAL: Uses מֵאֵשׁ הַשְּׁאוֹל ('from the fire of Sheol', H7585). Greek has ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ τῇ καιομένῃ ('in the lake that burns'). Sheol (שאול) is the Hebrew underworld — a deeply rooted OT concept (Gen 37:35, Num 16:30, Deut 32:22, Ps 16:10, 86:13, Isa 14:9). A back-translator from Greek 'lake' (λίμνη) would write אֲגַם אֵשׁ ('lake of fire'), NOT 'fire of Sheol.' The 'lake of fire' is a Greek concept; 'fire of Sheol' is a Hebrew one.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list: unbelievers, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, liars (5 categories). Greek list: cowardly, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, IDOLATERS, all liars (8 categories). Greek adds cowardly (δειλοῖς), abominable (ἐβδελυγμένοις), and idolaters (εἰδωλολάτραις).
Hebrew: 'fire of Sheol.' Greek: 'lake of fire.' Entirely different imagery.
translation_notes: כַּזְבָנִים (kazbanim — 'liars') is a later Hebrew agentive form from כזב (kazav — to lie). No standard Strong's number.
'Wages' for sechar captures the Hebrew concept of earned recompense — you labored in evil, here is your pay.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:22 — 'For a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol.' The Hebrew concept of fire in Sheol has deep OT roots. The Greek 'lake of fire' concept appears to be a reinterpretation.

verses.translation: And one{H259} of the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} came{H935} to me, who had in their hand{H3027} the bowls{H7086} full{H4392} of the seven{H7651} last{H314} plagues{H5061}, and he said{H559} to me: Come{H935} and see{H7200} the woman{H802}, the bride{H3618} of the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues/afflictions', H5061) — the specific Levitical word for plagues of Egypt (Ex 11:1) and skin diseases requiring priestly inspection (Lev 13-14). Greek πληγῶν ('blows/plagues') is generic. A back-translator could use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows/plagues') but the author specifically chose the Levitical term.

Uses שֶׂה (seh — 'lamb', H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek ἀρνίον is a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves) or טָלֶה (taleh). The use of seh ties the Lamb directly to the Passover.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman, the bride' (אשה then כלה). Greek: 'the bride, the woman' (νύμφην then γυναῖκα). Reversed order.
translation_notes: 'Plagues' for nega'im — preserving the Levitical/Exodus connection.
'Lamb' for seh — the Passover-specific term, distinguishing it from generic words for sheep.

verses.translation: And he led{H5090} me upon one{H259} mountain{H2022} which was great{H1419} and high{H1364}, and showed{H7200} me the great{H1419} city{H5892}, the holy{H6918} city{H5892} Yerushalayim{H3389}, descending{H3381} from the heavens{H8064} to the earth{H776}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'he led me' (ונהג אותי). Greek: 'he carried me away in the spirit' (ἀπήνεγκέ με ἐν πνεύματι). Greek adds 'in the spirit' which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'from heavens to the earth.' Greek: 'from heaven from God' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ). Again, Greek adds 'from God.'
translation_notes: נִהַג (nihag, H5090) means 'to lead/drive/guide' — used of leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6) and driving chariots. Concrete and physical, unlike the Greek 'carried away in spirit.'
textual_notes: Echoes Ezekiel 40:2 — 'he brought me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city.' The great and high mountain vision is an Ezekiel pattern.

verses.translation: And the splendor{H8597} of YHWH{H3068} was upon her, and her luminary{H3974} was like the light{H216} of the goodly{H2896} stone{H68} called{H7121} jasper.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְאוֹרָהּ (me'orah — 'her luminary', H3974) — the SAME word from Genesis 1:14-16 for the sun, moon, and stars (מְאֹרֹת). The New Jerusalem's light is described using creation language. Greek φωστήρ could be translated several ways; a back-translator would more likely use אוֹר (or — 'light') or נֵר (ner — 'lamp').

Uses אֶבֶן טוֹבָה ('goodly stone') — the standard OT term for precious gems (Gen 2:12, 1 Kings 10:2). Greek has λίθῳ τιμιωτάτῳ ('most precious stone'). A back-translator would use אבן יקרה ('precious stone'), not the OT-specific אבן טובה.
greek_deviations: Greek adds κρυσταλλίζοντι ('crystal-clear/sparkling') which is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Luminary' for ma'or preserves the Genesis creation connection — the same word for the heavenly lights.
'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) captures the beauty/glory/ornamental nuance that 'glory' alone misses.

verses.translation: And she had a great{H1419} wall{H2346} and twelve{H8147}{H6240} gates{H8179}, and at the gates{H8179} twelve{H8147}{H6240} messengers{H4397}, and twelve{H8147}{H6240} names{H8034} from the twelve{H8147}{H6240} tribes{H7626} of Yisrael{H3478}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds 'and high' (καὶ ὑψηλόν) to describe the wall — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'of Yisrael.' Greek: 'of the sons of Israel' (τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ). Greek adds 'sons of.'
Greek: names 'inscribed/written' (ἐπιγεγραμμένα). Hebrew just says 'names' without specifying they were written.
translation_notes: Note the gender mismatch: חוֹמָה (feminine) with גְּדוֹלִים (masculine plural). This may indicate 'great walls' as a composite structure, or it may be a textual peculiarity.
textual_notes: Echoes Ezekiel 48:30-35 which describes gates named after the twelve tribes.

verses.translation: From the east{H4217} three{H7969} gates{H8179}, and from the west{H4628} three{H7969}, and from the north{H6828} three{H7969}, and from the south{H1864} three{H7969}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew order: East, West, North, South. Greek order: East, North, South, West. The Hebrew follows a Hebrew-centric orientation where East (mizrach — 'place of rising') is primary, then its opposite West, then North-South. A back-translator from Greek would preserve the Greek order.
greek_deviations: Direction order differs: Hebrew E-W-N-S vs. Greek E-N-S-W.
textual_notes: Matches Ezekiel 48:30-34 which lists gates by direction, though Ezekiel's order is also different (N-E-S-W).

verses.translation: And the wall{H2346} of the city{H5892} had twelve{H8147}{H6240} foundations{H3247}, and on them were written{H3789} the names{H8034} of the twelve{H8147}{H6240} sent-ones{H7971} of the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׁלוּחִים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones', from shalach H7971) — a native Hebrew word meaning 'emissaries/delegates.' Greek has ἀποστόλων ('apostles'). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would almost certainly transliterate as אפוסטולים. The use of the native Hebrew sheluchim strongly suggests Hebrew priority.
translation_notes: 'Sent-ones' for sheluchim — preserving the Hebrew meaning without importing the Greek loanword 'apostle.'

verses.translation: And the one who spoke{H1696} with me had in his hand{H3027} one{H259} reed{H7070} of gold{H2091}, to measure{H4058} with it the city{H5892} and the wall{H2346} and the gates{H8179}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: city, wall, gates. Greek: city, gates, wall. Different order.
translation_notes: קָנֶה (qaneh, H7070 — 'reed') — the same word used for Ezekiel's measuring reed (Ezek 40:3,5). The vision deliberately parallels Ezekiel's temple measurement.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 40:3 — 'a man whose appearance was like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed (קנה) in his hand.' Same tool, different material (gold here vs. unspecified in Ezekiel).

verses.translation: And the city{H5892} lay at rest, squared, and its length{H753} was as its width{H7341}. And he measured{H4058} the city{H5892} with the reed{H7070}: twelve{H8147}{H6240} thousand{H505} field-plots, and its length{H753} and width{H7341} and height{H1364} of the city{H5892} are equal{H7737}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קִבְרוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה ('field-plots') as the unit of measurement. Greek has σταδίων ('stadia' — a Greek unit). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as סטאדיון or use a standard Hebrew measure like אמה (cubit). The Hebrew uses a uniquely Hebraic land-measurement idiom that has no connection to the Greek unit. The Greek translator converted the unfamiliar Hebrew unit to a familiar Greek one.

Uses מוּנָּח (munach — 'resting/placed', from nuach H5117 — to rest). This is the root of Noah's name and carries connotations of sabbath rest. Greek κεῖται ('lies/is situated') is neutral. A back-translator from Greek would use שוכב (shochev) or מונח is possible but the nuach/rest theological layer would be accidental.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'twelve thousand field-plots' (קברות השדה). Greek: 'twelve thousand stadia' (σταδίων). Entirely different measurement unit.
translation_notes: קִבְרוֹת (qivrot) — possibly related to measured burial plots (from קבר, qever — 'grave/plot') used as a land-area unit. Compare Kibroth-hattaavah (Num 11:34). The meaning is 'measured field sections.'
'Lay at rest' for munach captures the nuach/rest theology.

verses.translation: And its walls{H2346} were a hundred{H3967} and forty{H705}-four{H702} cubits{H520}, according to the measure{H4060} of a man{H120} which the messenger{H4397} had.
And the wall{H2346} was of jasper{H3471}, and the city{H5892} of pure{H2889} gold{H2091}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds ὅμοιον ὑάλῳ καθαρῷ ('like clear glass') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew is more concise.

verses.translation: And the foundations{H3247} of the wall{H2346} and of the city{H5892} were adorned with goodly{H2896} stones{H68}: the first{H7223} foundation{H3247} was jasper{H3471}, the second{H8145} sapphire{H5601}, and the third{H7992} chalcedony (in foreign tongue), and the fourth{H7243} turquoise{H5306}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The text explicitly marks קאלקידניר as בְּלַעַז ('in a foreign tongue'). A Hebrew author encountering a stone without a Hebrew name self-consciously flags it as foreign. A back-translator from Greek would simply transliterate without this meta-linguistic awareness. This is one of the strongest proofs of Hebrew authorship in the entire chapter.

Uses נֹפֶךְ (nofech, H5306) for the fourth stone — the High Priest's breastplate stone from Exodus 28:18 and 39:11. Greek has σμάραγδος ('emerald'). A back-translator would transliterate σμάραγδος, not reach back to the Torah's priestly gemstone vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Stone identifications differ between Hebrew and Greek for several positions, suggesting independent traditions rather than translation.
translation_notes: Preserving '(in foreign tongue)' as it appears in the Hebrew — this is part of the original text's self-awareness about borrowing non-Hebrew terms.
'Goodly stones' (אבנים טובים) rather than 'precious stones' — the Hebrew uses טוב ('good') not יקר ('precious'), matching OT usage (Gen 2:12).
textual_notes: The use of Torah breastplate stone names (Exodus 28:17-20) shows the author connecting the New Jerusalem's foundations to the priestly garments — the city itself becomes a priestly structure.

verses.translation: And the fifth{H2549} ruby{H124}, and the sixth{H8345} onyx{H7718}, and the seventh{H7637} crystal{H306}, and the eighth{H8066} chrysolite{H8658}, and the ninth{H8671} topaz{H6357}, and the tenth{H6224} agate{H7618}, and the eleventh{H6249}{H6240} jacinth{H3958}, and the twelfth{H8147}{H6240} is called{H7121} in foreign tongue amethyst.

one_way_hebrew: ALL stone names are from the High Priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20): אֹדֶם (odem), שֹׁהַם (shoham), אַחְלָמָה (achlamah), תַּרְשִׁישׁ (tarshish), פִּטְדָה (pitdah), שְׁבוֹ (shevo), לֶשֶׁם (leshem). These are Torah-specific gemstone vocabulary. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Greek names (σαρδόνυξ, σάρδιος, χρυσόλιθος, βήρυλλος, τοπάζιον, χρυσόπρασος, ὑάκινθος), not independently reconstruct the Exodus breastplate vocabulary.
Again marks the final stone בְּלַעַז ('in foreign tongue') — a second instance of the Hebrew author's meta-linguistic self-awareness.
greek_deviations: Stone identifications do not match Greek 1:1. E.g., Hebrew 5th = אדם (ruby/carnelian); Greek 5th = σαρδόνυξ (sardonyx). Hebrew 6th = שהם (onyx); Greek 6th = σάρδιος (sardius/carnelian). This suggests independent tradition.
translation_notes: Stone name identifications follow the standard OT identifications from Exodus. The exact modern mineral correspondence is debated for several of these.
textual_notes: The full breastplate stone list in Exodus 28:17-20: Row 1: אדם, פטדה, ברקת. Row 2: נפך, ספיר, יהלם. Row 3: לשם, שבו, אחלמה. Row 4: תרשיש, שהם, ישפה. The Hebrew Revelation redistributes these across twelve foundations.

verses.translation: And the twelve{H8147}{H6240} gates{H8179} were of pearls{H4026}, and every{H3605} single{H259} gate{H8179} was of one{H259} pearl. And the plazas{H7339} of the city{H5892} were of pure{H2889} gold{H2091}, like a clear{H2134} flask.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has πλατεῖα (singular 'street'). The Hebrew naturally uses plural for a city's public spaces.

Uses צְלוֹחִית (tselochit — 'flask/vial') where Greek has ὕαλος ('glass'). A back-translator from Greek would use זכוכית (zechuchit — 'glass'), not the Hebrew word for a vessel/flask. Different metaphor entirely.
translation_notes: זַךְ (zach, H2134 — 'pure/clear') is an OT word (Job 8:6, Prov 16:2, 20:11, Lam 4:7).

verses.translation: And I did not see{H7200} in her a house of prayer{H8605}, for YHWH{H3068} of Hosts{H6635} was the house{H1004} of their sanctuary{H4720}, and the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses TWO different terms: בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer', H8605) for what was NOT seen, and בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ ('house of the sanctuary', H4720) for what YHWH IS. Greek uses ναός ('temple') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word ναός twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes between a prayer house (synagogue-type) and the actual sanctuary (mikdash).

Uses יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tsevaot — 'YHWH of Hosts/Armies', H6635) — a specific compound divine name occurring 285 times in the OT. Greek has κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or similar, NOT the specific OT name YHWH Tsevaot.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7 — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְּפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13.
'House of the sanctuary' (beit hamikdash) is the standard Hebrew term for the Temple.

verses.translation: And the city{H5892} has no need of light{H216} from the sun{H8121} or from the moon{H3394}, for the splendor{H8597} of YHWH{H3068} is a luminary{H3974} for them, and its light{H216} is the lamb{H7716}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'its light is the lamb' (אורה — 'light'). Greek: 'its lamp (λύχνος) is the Lamb.' Hebrew uses אוֹר (elemental light); Greek uses λύχνος (a household lamp). Different scale of imagery.
translation_notes: מָאוֹר (ma'or, H3974) again — the Genesis 1:14-16 creation word. YHWH's glory replaces the sun and moon as the city's luminary, just as the luminaries served in the original creation.
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:19-20 — 'The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but YHWH will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.' The Hebrew preserves this Isaiah connection directly.

verses.translation: And the holy{H6918} peoples{H5971} walk{H1980} in this light{H216}, and the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} bring{H935} their resources{H2428} into her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָעַמִּים הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('the holy peoples', H6918). Greek has τὰ ἔθνη τῶν σωζομένων ('the nations of those being saved'). 'Holy peoples' (amim kedoshim) echoes the OT concept of a 'holy nation' (goy kadosh, Ex 19:6) extended to plural peoples. A back-translator from Greek would write העמים הנושעים ('the saved peoples'), not 'the holy peoples.'

Uses חֵילָם (cheilam — 'their resources/wealth/strength', H2428). Greek has δόξαν καὶ τιμήν ('glory and honor'). The Hebrew חיל encompasses wealth, military might, and productive capacity — an untranslatable Hebrew concept. A back-translator from Greek would use כבוד ויקר ('glory and honor').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy peoples.' Greek: 'saved nations.' Different qualifying attribute.
Hebrew: 'their resources' (one word — חיל). Greek: 'glory and honor' (two words). Different concepts entirely.
translation_notes: 'Resources' for chayil — this word covers wealth, military strength, valor, and productive capability. It's the word used in Proverbs 31:10 for the 'woman of chayil.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:3,5 — 'Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising... the wealth (חיל) of the nations shall come to you.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes Isaiah 60 with the same word חיל.

verses.translation: And your gates{H8179} shall be open{H6605} continually{H8548}; day{H3119} and night{H3915} they shall not be shut{H5462}, for there shall not be night{H3915}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 60:11 — וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִסָּגֵרוּ. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact words INCLUDING the 2nd person address שְׁעָרַיִךְ ('YOUR gates' — feminine singular suffix). Greek has αὐτῆς ('HER gates' — 3rd person). A back-translator from Greek, which has 3rd person 'its/her gates,' would NEVER switch to 2nd person 'your gates.' This is perhaps the single clearest one-way translation marker in the entire chapter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your gates' (2nd person, quoting Isaiah). Greek: 'its gates' (3rd person).
Hebrew: 'day and night they shall not be shut' (preserving Isaiah's full phrase). Greek: only 'by day' (ἡμέρας) — drops 'and night.'
translation_notes: Translated in 2nd person to preserve the Isaiah quotation: 'your gates shall be open continually.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:11 (exact source text): וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִסָּגֵרוּ לְהָבִיא אֵלַיִךְ חֵיל גּוֹיִם — 'And your gates shall be open continually; day and night they shall not be shut, to bring to you the wealth of nations.' The next verse (v26) fulfills the second half of this Isaiah prophecy.

verses.translation: And they shall bring{H935} into her splendor{H8597} and glory{H3519} from the peoples{H5971}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: תפארת וכבוד ('splendor and glory'). Greek: δόξαν καὶ τιμήν ('glory and honor'). Different word pair. Hebrew tiferet ('splendor/beauty') ≠ Greek doxa ('glory'); Hebrew kavod ('glory/weight') ≠ Greek time ('honor').
textual_notes: Continues the Isaiah 60:11 fulfillment — the wealth/glory of nations being brought into the city.

verses.translation: And a stranger{H2114} shall not come near{H7126} to him; only those whose name{H8034} is written{H3789} in the scroll{H5612} of life{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זָר (zar — 'stranger/unauthorized one', H2114). This is the specific Torah term for someone not authorized to approach holy space — used in Numbers 1:51, 3:10, 3:38, 18:4, 18:7 for non-priests approaching the Tabernacle ('the stranger who comes near shall be put to death'). Greek has πᾶν κοινοῦν ('anything defiled/common'). A back-translator from Greek would write כל טמא ('anything unclean') or כל חול ('anything common'), NOT the Levitical-priestly term zar. The Hebrew author sees the New Jerusalem as sacred priestly space where the 'unauthorized' may not approach.

Uses יִקְרַב (yiqrav — 'shall come near/approach', H7126) — the specific priestly term for approaching the altar/holy place (Lev 1:3, 9:7, 16:1, Num 16:40, 18:3). Greek εἰσέλθῃ means simply 'enter.' A back-translator from Greek would use יבוא (yavo — 'enter'), not the priestly-approach verb qarav.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a stranger shall not come near to HIM' (אליו — masculine singular, possibly YHWH). Greek: 'anything defiled shall not enter into IT' (εἰς αὐτήν — feminine, the city). Different subject restriction (unauthorized person vs. defiled thing) and different referent (him vs. it).
Greek adds 'doing abomination and lying' (ποιοῦν βδέλυγμα καὶ ψεῦδος) — an expanded list absent from the concise Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the scroll of life' (ספר החיים). Greek: 'the book of life of the Lamb' (βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου). Greek adds 'of the Lamb.'
translation_notes: 'Stranger' for zar — this is NOT a xenophobic term but a priestly/Levitical concept about authorization to enter holy space. The New Jerusalem is the ultimate Holy of Holies.
'Come near' for yiqrav — the specific priestly approach verb, distinguishing this from merely 'entering.'
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 (Hebrew) — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living (ספר חיים).' The Hebrew phrase 'sefer hachayyim' connects to this OT precedent.
The masculine אליו ('to him') may refer to YHWH rather than the city, making this a statement about approaching God's presence — consistent with the Levitical zar restriction.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 21 in Hebrew draws massively from Isaiah 60 and the Torah's Tabernacle/priestly vocabulary. The Hebrew text preserves exact OT quotations (Isaiah 25:8, 60:11), uses Torah-specific terminology (mishkan, seh, nega'im, zar, qarav, sheluchim, ma'or), and shows linguistic self-awareness (marking foreign loanwords with בלעז). The chapter contains at least 15 clear one-way translation markers — cases where the Hebrew could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The most striking are: (1) 'the first and the last' vs. 'Alpha and Omega,' (2) the verbatim Isaiah 60:11 quote with 2nd person address, (3) 'fire of Sheol' vs. 'lake of fire,' (4) the בלעז foreign-word markers, and (5) the zar/qarav priestly terminology in verse 27.
